children.text: Mount Kitanglad is a dormant volcano in Bukidnon that rises 2,899 m above sea level, the fourth-highest mountain in the Philippines. It lies inside a protected area that shelters mossy forest and Philippine eagle habitat, so climbers need a permit and an Indigenous ritual before a serious two-day, one-night ascent.
Mount Kitanglad is a dormant volcano in Bukidnon province in north-central Mindanao, standing about

above sea level. It ranks among the Philippines' high peaks alongside Mount Apo, Mount Dulang-dulang and Mount Pulag, and Wikipedia lists it as the fourth-highest mountain in the country. Some sources give other figures such as 2,938 m, which are generally thought to be mixed up with the neighboring Mount Dulang-dulang. The Spanish reportedly called it Mount Alanguilan, and the mountain straddles several municipalities, including Malaybalay, Lantapan, Impasug-ong, Sumilao and Libona.

The mountain is the heart of Mount Kitanglad Range Natural Park. It became a natural park by presidential proclamation in 1996, was confirmed as a protected area by law (RA 8978) in 2000, and was named an ASEAN Heritage Park in 2009. More than 600 rare and endemic species live here, including the critically endangered Philippine eagle, which nests in the forest, and rare plants such as Rafflesia. For that reason it is not an open tourist site: you need an entry permit from the Protected Area Management Board (PAMB).

The area is also the ancestral land of the Bukidnon, Higaonon and Talaandig peoples. Before the climb, a village elder performs a traditional ritual, and it is not a show for visitors but the procedure through which entry is granted. It is hard to find another Philippine climb where culture and conservation are so closely tied together.

The trail is mostly uphill. The Intavas route, known as the easiest, starts from a village at the foot of the mountain, passes through forest and mossy forest, and reaches a bunkhouse near the summit. Most climbers go up on the first day, watch the sunrise on the second morning and then descend. Communication towers stand at the summit and the nights are bitterly cold. This is not an easy mountain and it demands fitness and preparation, but dawn above a sea of clouds is one of the great rewards of climbing in Mindanao. Before you start, tell your guide honestly how you feel and what the weather looks like, and if the guide says to turn back, follow that advice. Getting home safely matters far more than one summit photo.

From the top you can see the Bukidnon plateau and the surrounding ranges in one sweep, and on a clear day even Mount Dulang-dulang beyond the ridge. Communication towers stand around the summit, so it is not an untouched peak, but the view is still stunning.

As you gain altitude, tree trunks and rocks are covered in thick moss. When fog rolls in the atmosphere becomes even more mysterious. This section is damp and full of exposed roots, so watch your footing, as it can be slippery.

The range's natural park is known as a nesting place for the Philippine eagle, the national bird. With luck you may see one soaring, but there is no guarantee. The basic courtesy here is not to disturb wildlife.

Before departure a village elder (datu) performs a traditional ritual in which chickens are offered, and climbers take part by placing a coin. It is a moment to tell the mountain's guardians that you are entering and to ask for safety, and it is an experience unique to this mountain.

blocks.title: A night at the summit bunkhouse

children.text: There is a bunkhouse near the summit, reportedly letting you sleep without a tent. It must be rented in advance, so confirm it ahead of time through your guide or operator. Temperatures drop sharply at night, so bring heavy clothing and a sleeping bag.

blocks.title: Sunrise and sea of clouds at dawn

children.text: On the second day you watch the sunrise from the summit at around 5 AM. Depending on the clouds, a sea of clouds may spread below. The weather is a matter of luck and a clear sky cannot be guaranteed.

blocks.title: Starting point for the Dulang-dulang traverse

children.text: Experienced mountaineers sometimes traverse from Kitanglad to Mount Dulang-dulang. The traverse in a single day is described as a demanding route taking 8–16 hours, and it is not recommended for first-time visitors.

The park is said to hold at least 185 species of trees and woody plants, and mammals such as bats, monkeys and colugos (flying lemurs) are reported to live here. Rare species such as the Philippine tarsier and Rafflesia schadenbergiana are also mentioned for this area. If you stop and listen to the forest, you will find a stillness that is hard to come by in the lowlands.

items.title: Two-day summit climb
items.subtitle: From Intavas, one night at the summit bunkhouse

children.text: At the PAMB office in Impasug-ong you complete permit paperwork and a safety briefing (orientation). Depending on the operator it is held the day before at around
, and you need a list with each climber's name, age, gender and address.
In the village of Intavas, La Fortuna, you take part in the traditional ritual and stay overnight. Some places charge an extra of around
for the stay.
Wake up early and set out with your guide. Part of the way to the trailhead is covered by motorcycle (habal-habal).
Lunch and a rest near a wide rock. The trail is mostly uphill, so climb slowly at a steady pace.
Reach the bunkhouse near the summit, unpack and have dinner. Temperatures fall quickly after sunset, so put on warm clothes right away.
Watch the sunrise from the summit. On a clear day you can see the sea of clouds and the ridge of Mount Dulang-dulang.
Have breakfast and start the descent. One itinerary describes the return to Intavas as taking about
6 hours
This schedule is an example based on an itinerary published by an operator. For how permits are issued and the exact times, check the latest announcements from the PAMB and your operator.

children.text: Gather in Davao and set off by van toward Malaybalay. The trip is described as taking about
5–6 hours
Arrive in Intavas, have breakfast and hold the ritual at around
Start the climb. You have lunch on the trail and reach the area near the summit at around 3 PM.
After breakfast you descend, have lunch at an elder's house in the village, and return to Davao in the afternoon.
There are direct flights from Manila (NAIA) to Laguindingan Airport (CGY) in Cagayan de Oro. Flight times and airlines change with the season, so check the latest schedules.
You can also fly into Francisco Bangoy International Airport (DVO) in Davao and continue overland. The van ride from Davao to Intavas is described as taking about
5–6 hours

items.title: Bus and van from Cagayan de Oro

children.text: Buses and vans to Malaybalay and Valencia leave from the Agora terminal in Cagayan de Oro and take about
1–3 hours
. Malaybalay is about
91 km
from Cagayan de Oro.
Tell the driver in advance that you are getting off at Impasug-ong or the Intavas junction.
Malaybalay has no airport at present.
From the Intavas turnoff on the highway (Sayre Highway), a habal-habal (motorcycle taxi) takes about
30 minutes
to reach Intavas village. Some reports say the road is too rough for cars.
In an older report the fare was around
per person, so check the current fare locally.

Nearby Malaybalay gets rain year-round, with the most rain in April–September and the relatively driest months in January–March. Mountain weather is more changeable than in the lowlands, so fog or rain can arrive suddenly even in the dry season.
The area near the summit is very cold at night. If you pack light clothing based only on lowland temperatures, you will regret it.

Package itineraries often start at dawn, so resting the day before in Intavas village makes things easier. During holidays and school breaks permit slots fill up quickly, so contact an operator or the PAMB at least a few weeks ahead to fix your date.

On the mountain you sleep in the summit bunkhouse or in a tent. The bunkhouse has bunk beds and must be booked in advance, and electricity and water are limited, so bring plenty of drinking water and warm gear. The night before the climb, many people stay in Intavas village or in Impasug-ong or Malaybalay.
Packages often include five meals, and some operators ask you to bring your own utensils. Malaybalay has restaurants and a market that make it easy to eat before and after the climb, and nearby
Dahilayan
offers farms and leisure activities.

After the climb we recommend recovering in Malaybalay with hot soup and local dishes. Bukidnon is a highland area that is cooler than the lowlands and rich in vegetables and farm produce. On the trail, pack light, high-calorie snacks such as trail food, chocolate and nuts.
A PAMB permit and the traditional ritual are required. Entering without a permit can lead to fines under the law, so always follow the procedure.
If it is your first time, go with a personal guide or an operator. There are reports that a group is limited to about 15 people.
Prepare for the night temperatures near the summit with thick warm clothing, a windproof jacket and a sleeping bag.
Carry plenty of water. An older report mentions one climber carrying about 3.5 liters.
For rain, bring a waterproof jacket, a waterproof pack cover and hiking shoes with good grip.
Carry all your trash back out. The rule is to leave nothing on the mountain.
Do not rashly attempt the Dulang-dulang traverse. The one-day traverse is extremely tiring and there have been cases of descending in the dark.
Signal is weak, so carry offline maps and a power bank, and let family or friends know your plans.
Wear well broken-in hiking boots, and spare socks and gloves help against the cold at dawn.
If you arrive in Cagayan de Oro, it is safer to stay the night before in Malaybalay to loosen up.
Mount Kitanglad is a protected area, so you cannot enter without a PAMB permit and the Indigenous ritual, and entering without a permit is punishable.
Permit, ritual and guide requirements and prices can change from year to year, so check the latest announcements with the PAMB or your operator before departure.
This is a serious climb that is mostly uphill and dangerous if your fitness is low. If you lack hiking experience, practice first on lower mountains.
Near the summit it is cold enough to risk hypothermia. Change out of wet clothes immediately.
In the rainy season the trail turns to mud and visibility worsens. If heavy rain is forecast, postpone the trip.
Respect the Indigenous elders and village rules. If photos or behavior might cause offense, ask first.
Phone signal and internet are weak in many sections. Do not separate from your group and follow your guide's instructions.

A farm and leisure complex at the foot of the mountains, easy to drop by before or after the climb.
